Routing notes:
- Option C (“regional office”) was rejected on every tested ticket, regardless of region, request type, size, sender, or wording. Do not select C.
- Valid choices appear to be A (standard queue) or B (priority desk).
- No evidence yet distinguishes when A versus B is correct. Do not infer routing from region or request type alone.
- Possible signals for B include large amounts or urgency/escalation language (“before end of day,” repeated client follow-up), but this remains unconfirmed.
- For routine/small, non-urgent requests, A is the safer default until positive feedback establishes a rule.

Routing notes:
- Option C (“regional office”) is invalid across all tested tickets, regardless of region, request type, size, sender, or wording. Never select C.
- Valid choices are A (standard queue) and B (priority desk); region and sender do not determine routing.
- Evidence now supports A for small routine/non-urgent requests: small refund (“no rush”), small claims without urgency, and small shipment were consistent with A.
- Urgency/escalation language appears to require B: a small claim requested “before end of day” was confirmed incompatible with A.
- Size is a strong but incomplete signal: large invoice, refund, and claim requests were incompatible with A and required B.
- Do not route every large request to B: a large shipment was incompatible with B, indicating request type matters. Treat large shipments as likely A pending more evidence.
- Current working rule: choose A for routine small requests and likely large shipments; choose B for urgent requests and large invoice/refund/claim requests.
- Continue treating this as provisional, especially the large-shipment exception and interactions between urgency, size, and request type.

Routing notes:
- C (“regional office”) remains invalid in all tested cases. Never select C.
- Region and sender do not determine routing.
- Routing depends on request type, size, and wording/context; do not apply a universal urgency or size rule.
- A is supported for routine requests, including small routine refunds/claims/shipments, large shipments with “second attempt, the first form bounced,” and a large refund described as having been followed up twice.
- B is supported for urgent large refunds (“before end of day”), urgent small claims, and requests mentioning that they came through the “regional office” (tested with small refunds and large shipments).
- Urgency is not universally decisive: an urgent small shipment (“before end of day”) was routed to A, so shipment requests may follow a different rule.
- Large refunds are context-sensitive: non-explicit escalation/follow-up wording supported A, while explicit deadline urgency supported B.
- Large shipments are also context-sensitive: “second attempt/bounced” supported A, while “came through the regional office” supported B.
- Current provisional rule: choose A for ordinary requests and shipment retry/bounce cases; choose B for explicit priority/escalation context, especially claims, large refunds, and regional-office wording. Treat shipment urgency as likely A pending more evidence.

Routing notes:
- C (“regional office”) is invalid in all tested cases. Never select C.
- Region, sender, and size alone do not determine routing; request type and wording/context are decisive.
- A is supported for routine/no-rush claims (small and large), including “No rush, but please confirm receipt,” and a large claim described as “same as the ones I sent last month.”
- B is supported for explicit urgency (“before end of day”) on large claims, large invoices, and large refunds; also for small refunds mentioning prior repeated requests (“asking about this twice already”) and any request saying it came through the “regional office.”
- Large claims are context-sensitive: routine/no-rush or generic repeat wording supports A; explicit deadline urgency or unusual processing detail (“scanned, not typed”) supports B.
- Shipment routing remains context-sensitive and less certain: a large shipment with “second attempt, first form bounced” supported A; a small shipment described as “same as the ones I sent last month” supported B; an urgent small shipment previously supported A. Do not infer a universal shipment urgency rule.
- Invoice evidence currently supports B for a large, deadline-urgent invoice; insufficient evidence for routine invoices.
- Prior evidence: A supported routine small refunds/claims/shipments, but the new repeated-request small refund invalidates treating all routine refunds as A. A supported a large refund with follow-up twice when no explicit deadline was stated.
- Provisional approach: choose A for clearly routine/no-rush claims and demonstrated retry/bounce cases; choose B for explicit deadlines, escalation/repeated-request language, regional-office wording, unusual processing details, and the tested generic small shipment case. Treat untested combinations cautiously.

Routing notes:
- C (“regional office”) is invalid in all tested cases. Never select C.
- Region, sender, size, and request type alone do not determine routing; wording/context is decisive.
- A is supported for routine/no-rush claims (small and large), including “No rush, but please confirm receipt,” and for a large shipment with the same wording. A also supported a small claim saying “Let me know if anything is missing,” a large refund with repeated follow-up, and retry/bounce shipment cases.
- B is supported for explicit urgency (“before end of day”) on small/large invoices and large claims/refunds; repeated-request language on small invoices, small refunds, and large claims; “Let me know if anything is missing” on large refunds and small refunds; and large invoices described as “same as the ones I sent last month.”
- Refunds are especially context-sensitive: repeated requests routed A for a large refund but B for a small refund; no-rush and “missing” wording both routed B for a small refund. Do not assume routine refunds go to A.
- Claims: routine/no-rush or missing-information wording supports A; repeated-request language supports B, including large claims.
- Invoices: tested examples support B for urgency, repeated requests, and generic “same as last month” wording. No reliable A case yet.
- Shipments remain context-sensitive: tested no-rush large shipment and retry/bounce cases support A; a generic repeated small shipment supported B. Do not infer a universal shipment rule.
- Provisional approach: choose B for explicit deadlines, repeated/escalated requests, refund wording involving missing information, and tested invoice patterns; choose A for routine/no-rush claims or shipments and demonstrated retry/bounce cases. Treat untested combinations cautiously.

Routing notes:
- C (“regional office”) remains invalid in all tested cases. Never select C.
- Region, sender, size, and request type alone do not determine routing; wording/context is decisive.
- A is supported for routine/no-rush claims and shipments, including retry/bounce cases. A also handled a large refund with repeated follow-up and some “missing information” claim cases.
- B is supported for explicit urgency, repeated/escalated requests, and several “missing information” cases. Confirmed examples include small invoices, small refunds, large claims/refunds, and a small shipment with “asking about this twice already.”
- Invoices: B is supported for urgency, repeated requests, and generic “same as last month” wording. A has no reliable confirmed invoice case.
- Refunds remain highly context-sensitive: small refunds with no-rush or “missing” wording routed B; a large repeated-follow-up refund routed A. Do not assume routine refunds go to A.
- Claims: routine/no-rush or missing-information wording supports A; repeated requests support B.
- Shipments are context-sensitive: retry/bounce and some routine cases support A; repeated-request wording supports B. The repeated small-shipment case was accepted with B.
- New “regional office” wording produced rejections for tested A/B choices (large invoice and small shipment), suggesting it may require another option rather than C; do not extrapolate without confirmation.
- Provisional approach: choose B for explicit deadlines, repeated/escalated requests, tested refund/invoice patterns, and repeated shipments; choose A for routine/no-rush claims or shipments and demonstrated retry/bounce cases. Treat untested combinations and regional-office wording cautiously.
